Decadent

DEK-uh-dunt -- Latin de- ('down') plus cadere ('to fall'): pleasure so heavy that standards fall down under it. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Decadent is luxuriously self-indulgent, and sometimes morally corrupt.

The emperor's decadent banquets lasted three days and emptied the treasury.

Worked Example

A weekend package includes a marble bath filled with rose petals, a private chef for every meal, and gold-flecked truffles delivered to the room at midnight.

Comfort and pleasure piled far past what anyone actually needs is exactly what decadent describes. It can also carry a sharper edge: calling a society decadent suggests all that indulgence has left it soft and corrupt.

How Decadent Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

indulgent

indulgent: freely giving in to pleasure

dissolute

dissolute: given over to pleasure and loose living

luxurious

luxurious: rich, comfortable, and expensive

Antonyms

restrained

restrained: holding back from excess

modest

modest: plain and not extravagant

How Strong Is It? — indulgent → decadent → dissolute

indulgent vs. decadent

indulgent vs. decadent: Indulgent is the gentler word -- an indulgent dessert is just a treat, while decadent suggests indulgence taken to an eyebrow-raising extreme.

dissolute vs. decadent

dissolute vs. decadent: Dissolute is decadent at its harshest: decadent can be a playful compliment about a chocolate cake, while dissolute is a flat moral judgment about a wasted, pleasure-soaked life.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — de-

prefix — de-: down (Latin)

root — -cad-

root — -cad-: to fall (Latin (cadere))

suffix — -ent

suffix — -ent: adjective-forming: doing the action (Latin (-entem))

Put it together

Put it together: Medieval Latin decadentia meant 'a falling away,' from de- ('down') and cadere ('to fall') -- a decadent society has fallen from its old standards into easy pleasure, from the same cad- root that gives us cascade and decay.

Root Check

Word Choice

Decadent has two moods. About food it is nearly a compliment -- a decadent dessert is gloriously rich. About people, empires, or eras it is an accusation, suggesting that comfort has rotted away discipline and morals.
